extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, satirical essayists, and educated readers interested in poetry and humorous/satirical composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on judging and composing characters in heroic/epic poetry and on techniques of satirical/humorous composition as exemplified in Addison and Steele's Spectator essays. Focuses on character variety, novelty, probability, audience relation, and satirical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and novelty of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The epic should present a multitude and variety of characters; characters should be novel where the subject allows (Homer 'excelled ... in the Multitude and Variety of his Characters').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide many distinct persons, each suited to particular parts of the story; novelty (unique ages, origins, or types) adds splendour to an heroic poem. Avoid sameness among characters; variety is a central merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters distinguished by manners as well as station
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character should be as distinguishable by their manners and ways of speaking as by their dominions or names ('His Princes are as much distinguished by their Manners, as by their Dominions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters' speech and actions so particular that a reader could ascribe a speech or deed to the person without seeing the name; cultivate distinctive voices and behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and dignity appropriate to a heroic poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters in an epic should possess a dignity and often a novelty fitting the grandeur of the subject ('a certain Dignity as well as Novelty, which adapts them in a more peculiar manner to the Nature of an Heroic Poem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce figures (even extraordinary or unusual ones) that lend grandeur and singularity to the poem; balance novelty with an elevated tone suitable to heroics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allegorical or shadowy persons (and their limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical beings (e.g., Sin and Death in Paradise Lost) can be introduced to enlarge a poem's cast when the human dramatis personae are few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory can enrich the fable and supply variety, but chimerical or unsubstantial beings risk lacking required probability for an epic; employ such figures carefully and ensure they act in suitably 'probable' or fitting ways when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability/credibility of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and heroic writings require a measure of probability attached to characters and actions; wholly unsubstantial beings may fail this test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when introducing supernatural or allegorical figures, maintain enough plausibility or internal consistency so readers accept them; avoid figures whose conduct violates the expected probability of the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience identification through choice of hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing a hero related to the poem's intended audience (Achilles to Greeks, Æneas to Romans) increases readers' sympathy and engagement with the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, select protagonists with natural ties or representative value to your readers to heighten emotional investment; universal figures (as in Milton) can succeed by representing shared human stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety within similar character-types
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters of a similar nominal type (e.g., men of courage) should nonetheless differ in particular qualities and modes of excellence ('they differ from one another as to the particular kinds of Courage in which they excel').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate characters by subtypes, motives, temperaments, or specialized virtues so that even like roles feel distinct and interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate dignity and fit for divine/angelic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine or angelic persons should act and speak in manners suitable to their superior nature (e.g., Raphael shows 'Dignity and Condescension').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign behaviours, speech patterns, and roles to supernatural characters consistent with their status; avoid trivializing or miscasting such figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of virtue/infirmities to evoke pity and terror (Aristotelian point)
rubrics_metrics.description: A character of perfect virtue falling into misfortune excites pity but not terror; a person with virtue mixed with infirmities provokes both pity and terror because readers see likeness to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragic effect, portray protagonists with a mixture of excellence and fallibility so audiences can both pity and fear; avoid presenting wholly flawless figures for tragedy if the aim is to provoke terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of an absolutely perfect hero in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: An absolutely and consummately virtuous person should not be introduced in tragedy (it lessens tragic effect according to the essay's reading of Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure tragic protagonists possess some human frailty or complexity to make their reversals moving and plausible to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-heroic and allegory as acceptable devices in appropriate contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mock-heroic poems and other imitative forms employ allegorical or personified figures effectively (examples: The Dispensary, The Lutrin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mock-heroic or satirical contexts, allegory and personification can be apt and beautiful; gauge genre expectations before transplanting those devices into stricter epic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical device — learned/technical parody
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodying scientific or learned discourse (e.g., a mock-dissection of a beau's head) yields humour by treating trivial social foibles with solemn technicality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the high-register language and apparatus of science or scholarship to describe petty or vain subjects, exposing vanity through disproportionate analytic seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical device — concrete, absurd inventories and hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour arises from detailed, concrete lists of absurd contents (ribbons in skull cavities, billets-doux in brain cells) and exaggerated imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ vivid, specific, and escalating absurd details to make satire tangible and laughable; the concreteness strengthens the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical device — witty renaming and etymological jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comically naming anatomical parts with mock-Latin or translated humorous functions (e.g., 'Musculi Amatorii' → 'Ogling Muscles') creates comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin plausible-sounding technical names and supply a plain-English gloss that undercuts pretension; the contrast between learned form and comic content is effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and discretion relative to audience sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should consider what is fit for particular listeners (example: wrapping indecent matters in Greek to avoid scandalizing ladies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauge audience composition and prudence: obscure or omit indecent detail when the audience requires decorum, or risk embarrassment; conversely, deliberate obscurity can be used to court select readers but may backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varying moral severity according to circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing vice (e.g., prostitution), one should temper severe language and consider mitigating circumstances (poverty, coercion, youth) rather than employing blanket condemnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In moral or satirical critique, differentiate between offenders, account for context, and modulate tone to avoid losing credibility through excessive invective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of correspondence and reader submissions as material (with adaptation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters from correspondents indicate which papers please readers and supply material for new speculations; the editor may change language or omit compliments as long as sense is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate submitted material: adapt for voice, omit irrelevant flattery, and reshape hints into original plans while preserving the core insight and respecting readers' sensibilities.
